citation: Tamim, R. M., Bernard, R. M., Borokhovski, E., Abrami, P. C., & Schmid, R. F. (2011). What forty years of research says about the impact of technology on learning: A second-order meta-analysis and validation study. Review of Educational Research, 81(1), 4-28. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654310393361

policy_or_intervention.mechanism: Instructional Technology Integration vs. Direct Delivery

theoretical_framing.udl_and_accessibility_considerations: Examines constructivist vs direct instruction applications across diverse learner populations.

findings_summary.effect_sizes_or_trends: Overall small to moderate positive effect (g = 0.35). Technology used to support cognitive construction yielded significantly higher effects than technology used for direct delivery/drill (g = 0.42 vs g = 0.16).
findings_summary.discrepancy_notes: Highlights that technology presence alone explains minimal variance; the pedagogical task design accounts for the majority of learning gains.

critical_limitations: Second-order meta-analysis summarizing pre-2010 studies; predates smartphones and generative AI.

citation: Zheng, B., Warschauer, M., Lin, C. H., & Chang, C. (2016). Learning in one-to-one laptop environments: A meta-analysis and research synthesis. Review of Educational Research, 86(4), 1052-1084. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654316628645

theoretical_framing.udl_and_accessibility_considerations: Noted benefits in student-centered writing and research across Title I and diverse student demographics.

findings_summary.effect_sizes_or_trends: Significant positive average effect sizes in English/language arts (d = 0.15), writing (d = 0.20), mathematics (d = 0.17), and science (d = 0.25).
findings_summary.discrepancy_notes: Program-level success depended heavily on teacher professional development, curriculum integration, and student writing practice rather than device ubiquity.

critical_limitations: Data spans 2001 to 2015; reflects an era prior to algorithmic feeds, social media saturation, and automated generative AI essay writers.

citation: Odgers, C. L., & Jensen, M. R. (2020). Annual research review: Adolescent mental health in the digital age: Facts, fears, and future directions. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 61(3), 336-348. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.13190

theoretical_framing.udl_and_accessibility_considerations: Demonstrates that digital platforms amplify existing offline vulnerabilities (economic hardship, family trauma, mental health history).

findings_summary.effect_sizes_or_trends: Associations between aggregate screen time and adolescent mental health symptoms are near-zero or clinically trivial (median r ≈ -0.05).
findings_summary.discrepancy_notes: Directly counters simplistic monocausal displacement narratives by showing that within-person variability and offline social context explain the majority of psychological risk.

critical_limitations: Focuses primarily on personal smartphones and social media rather than school-issued LMS or instructional software.

citation: Ministry of Education, Culture and Science. (2025). National evaluation of the mobile phone policy in Dutch secondary and primary schools. Government of the Netherlands.

theoretical_framing.udl_and_accessibility_considerations: Exemptions maintained for medical needs (e.g. glucose monitoring) and specific instructional tasks.

findings_summary.effect_sizes_or_trends: 75% of secondary schools reported perceived improvements in student concentration; 66% reported improved social atmosphere; only 33% observed measurable academic gains.
findings_summary.discrepancy_notes: Major divergence between high perceived social/attentional calm and modest measurable academic attainment gains.

critical_limitations: Relies predominantly on administrator and educator perceptual survey data rather than standardized longitudinal achievement metrics.

citation: Kieling, C., et al. (2024). The SMART Schools Study: Evaluating the impact of school smartphone policies on adolescent mental health and educational attainment. The Lancet Regional Health - Europe, 38, 100842. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100842

theoretical_framing.udl_and_accessibility_considerations: Controlled for socioeconomic deprivation index and baseline pupil health.

findings_summary.effect_sizes_or_trends: No statistically significant differences between schools with strict phone bans and schools with flexible policies across adolescent wellbeing, sleep quality, anxiety, or academic attainment.
findings_summary.discrepancy_notes: Contrasts sharply with popular policy assumptions that banning phones will automatically repair mental health metrics.

critical_limitations: Quasi-experimental observational design with potential unmeasured school-level cultural confounders.

citation: Government Offices of Sweden. (2024). Government investing in more reading time and less screen time: Reversing early digital mandates in preschool and primary education. Ministry of Education and Research.

theoretical_framing.udl_and_accessibility_considerations: Focus on early literacy development, neurodevelopmental handwriting practice, and tactile reading engagement.

findings_summary.effect_sizes_or_trends: Triggered by PIRLS 4th-grade reading scores declining from 555 (2016) to 544 (2021). National budget allocated ~€100M+ to guarantee physical textbooks for every student.
findings_summary.discrepancy_notes: Represents the purest national example of an instructional reversal (moving from digital apps back to physical print and handwriting) rather than a mere phone ban.

critical_limitations: Longitudinal achievement recovery data following the textbook reinvestment remains in progress.

citation: Global Education Monitoring Report Team. (2023). Technology in education: A tool on whose terms? UNESCO. https://doi.org/10.54675/QBKP7378

theoretical_framing.udl_and_accessibility_considerations: Highlights that 89% of 163 edtech products surveyed during pandemic remote learning infringed or risked children's data privacy.

findings_summary.effect_sizes_or_trends: Technology supports learning only when subordinate to human pedagogy; warns that uncritical digital adoption deepens inequality and diverts funding from foundational infrastructure.
findings_summary.discrepancy_notes: Frames the device debate around governance, privacy, and commercial surveillance rather than simplistic screen moral panics.

critical_limitations: Global scope spans highly disparate infrastructure contexts, from high-income 1:1 districts to low-resource classrooms without electricity.

citation: Lapin, H. A. (2015). Investigation of the Los Angeles Unified School District Common Core Technology Project and iPad deployment. Office of the Inspector General, LAUSD.

theoretical_framing.udl_and_accessibility_considerations: Purchased for $1.3B bond funding; Pearson digital curriculum was incomplete; devices bypassed within 48 hours; teacher professional learning was absent.

findings_summary.effect_sizes_or_trends: Complete program cancellation following procurement scandal, federal investigation, and student bypass of security profiles.
findings_summary.discrepancy_notes: Canonical case study illustrating that the most spectacular device failure in U.S. history was rooted in governance, vendor capture, and absent pedagogy rather than cognitive screen effects.

critical_limitations: Qualitative case study and investigative audit report; specific to procurement context of 2013-2015.

citation: Delgado, P., Vargas, C., Ackerman, R., & Salmeron, L. (2018). Don't throw away your printed books: A meta-analysis on the effects of reading media on reading comprehension. Educational Research Review, 25, 23-38. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.09.003

theoretical_framing.udl_and_accessibility_considerations: Screen inferiority effect was larger for informational texts and under time constraints.

findings_summary.effect_sizes_or_trends: Significant print advantage for reading comprehension (g = -0.21). The screen disadvantage increased over time (2000-2017), refuting the digital natives hypothesis.
findings_summary.discrepancy_notes: Shows that cognitive friction in linear reading is diminished on screens due to shallow skimming habits.

critical_limitations: Laboratory and classroom experimental tasks; did not evaluate modern adaptive e-readers with accessibility accommodations.
